Although most ciclosporin responders eventually lose response, most responders to ritlecitinib sustain clinical response at 24 months with treatment [ , ]. 1.5 Definition of Moderate to Severe Alopecia Areata The Severity of Alopecia Tool (SALT) is the standard metric used to quantify the extent of hair loss in phase 2 and phase 3 clinical trials of AA [ ]. A SALT score of 0 indicates no scalp hair loss, whereas a score of 100 represents complete loss of scalp hair [ , ]. Subscript numerals are used to denote percentage improvement from baseline. For example, SALT 50 reflects a 50% reduction in hair loss compared to baseline. The Alopecia Areata Investigator Global Assessment scale (AA‐IGA) (Table ) uses SALT as a singular measure to define disease severity. Specifically, a SALT score from 1 to 20 corresponds to limited disease; 21–49 to moderate disease; 50–94 to severe disease; and 95–100 to very severe disease (Table ) [ ]. These severity thresholds have been endorsed by a global expert consensus statement [ ]. There is expert consensus that AA patients with moderate to very severe disease are candidates for systemic therapy, and that systemic corticosteroids reduce the risk of disease progression and disease relapse [ , , ]. In the pivotal phase 3 trials for patients with a baseline SALT > 50 treated with either baricitinib or ritlecitinib, the primary outcome measure that was used to define a favourable treatment outcome was a SALT score of ≤ 20 [ ]. Various visual aids are available to facilitate calculation of the SALT score. The original aid created by Olsen et al. allows clinicians to map the area of hair loss in each quadrant. It is most useful for patients with moderate to very severe disease. The Sinclair SALT seven score card (Figure ) is a transparent business card with markings representing SALT scores of 0.125, 1, 2, 3 and 7, which can be placed on the scalp. It is particularly useful for rapid scoring of patients with limited or moderate disease [ ]. 2 Methods An initial exercise on reviewing current international and Australian guidelines for management of severe alopecia areata was conducted as well as a review of current literature. The grade of each therapy type was determined based on current data availability and assessed using the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Body of Evidence Matrix (Table ) [ ]. Subsequently, a summary of treatment types was categorised according to the NHMRC grading (Table ). Following this exercise, discussions with local Australian dermatologists with specific expertise in treating AA were held, and key areas of need were identified. An updated consensus statement for the management of chronic, moderate‐to‐severe AA was drafted from these discussions and disseminated to Australian dermatologists with a subspecialty in hair and scalp disorders for input. Treatment algorithms were developed to guide clinical decision‐making in alopecia areata (AA), incorporating current evidence, clinical experience and key disease characteristics. Two separate algorithms are presented: one for acute AA (disease duration < 6 months) (Figure ) and one for chronic or chronic persistent AA (Figure ). In a 2023 systematic review and meta‐analysis of seven randomised clinical trials with 1710 patients, JAK inhibitors were associated with patients achieving a 30%, 50% or 90% improvement in SALT scores from baseline compared with placebo. Results from notable large RCTs are outlined below. 3.1 Baricitinib Baricitinib is a selective inhibitor of JAK1 and 2 that is approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) for the treatment of severe and very severe alopecia areata in adults [ ]. It is also TGA approved for the treatment of atopic dermatitis and rheumatoid arthritis [ ]. In severe AA, Baricitinib is administered orally at a dosage of 2 mg once daily, which can be increased to 4 mg once daily in case of inadequate response. In very severe AA, therapy should be initiated at a dosage of 4 mg once daily, reduced to 2 mg once daily when an adequate response has been achieved [ ]. 3.1.1 Efficacy In the BRAVE‐AA1 and AA2 Phase 3 randomised clinical trials, 36.8%–40.9% of participants with severe or very severe AA treated with baricitinib 4 mg and 21.2%–24.4% of those treated with baricitinib 2 mg achieved a SALT score of ≤ 20 at 52 weeks. With continued treatment, that response (SALT score of ≤ 20) was maintained through to 152 weeks in 89.1% of participants treated with 4 mg daily and 83.6% of those who received 2 mg daily. A SALT score ≤ 10 was achieved by 27.8%–29.9% of participants treated with 4 mg and 14.1%–16.7% of those treated with 2 mg at 52 weeks [ , , ]. Outcome measures continued to improve after 18 and 26 months of treatment implying that long‐term therapy could be especially important for patients with extensive disease at baseline [ ]. A recent real‐world study found 61.5% (59 out of 96 patients) achieved a SALT score of ≤ 20 at the end of a 52‐week treatment period [ ]. 3.2 Ritlecitinib Ritlecitinib is a selective inhibitor of Janus kinase 3 (JAK3) and the tyrosine kinase expressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (TEC) family of kinases. It inhibits cytokine‐induced phosphorylation of signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) mediated by JAK3‐dependent cytokines, as well as blocking signalling of B and T‐cell receptors dependent on TEC kinase family members [ ]. Ritlecitinib was approved by the TGA for the treatment of severe AA in June 2024 in adults and adolescents 12 years and older. Ritlecitinib is administered orally at a dosage of 50 mg once daily [ , ]. 3.2.1 Efficacy An integrated analysis of the ALLEGRO Phase 2b/3 and long‐term Phase 3 studies found 45.1% of participants who received ritlecitinib 50 mg and 45.9% of those receiving 200 mg/50 mg (200 mg daily loading dose for 4 weeks followed by 50 mg daily dose) achieved a SALT score of ≤ 20 at Year 1. Additionally, a SALT score of ≤ 10 was achieved by 34.2% of participants on 50 mg and 39.4% on the 200 mg/50 mg regimen in the first year [ ]. A higher proportion of participants achieved a SALT score of ≤ 20 by Year 2. Participants with AT or AU or with longer episodes of severe disease, showed lower response rates. These findings suggest that earlier initiation of treatment may result in better outcomes [ , ]. A recent systematic review evaluated the efficacy and safety of ritlecitinib versus baricitinib, showing comparable efficacy of ritlecitinib 50 mg daily and baricitinib 4 mg [ ]. A comparison of side effects and laboratory investigation alterations reported with baricitinib and ritlecitinib in AA patients is described in Table . 3.3 Assessment of Response to JAKi Treatment Response to treatment is defined in current studies as achieving a SALT ≤ 20 with a secondary objective of achieving SALT ≤ 10. Response to treatment can also be evaluated by percentage of change from baseline. AT and AU patients might perceive achieving eyebrow, eyelash and beard regrowth as a reasonable treatment response despite the SALT score remaining unchanged. The area of scalp involvement, whether it be easy to conceal by parting hair a certain way or through adopting a different hairstyle, can significantly influence patient satisfaction. This cosmetic impact may determine whether a patient feels content or distressed, regardless of their SALT score. 3.4 Effect of Episode Duration on Response to Treatment Nearly 50% of patients with patchy alopecia areata persisting for over a

treatment can also be evaluated by percentage of change from baseline. AT and AU patients might perceive achieving eyebrow, eyelash and beard regrowth as a reasonable treatment response despite the SALT score remaining unchanged. The area of scalp involvement, whether it be easy to conceal by parting hair a certain way or through adopting a different hairstyle, can significantly influence patient satisfaction. This cosmetic impact may determine whether a patient feels content or distressed, regardless of their SALT score. 3.4 Effect of Episode Duration on Response to Treatment Nearly 50% of patients with patchy alopecia areata persisting for over a year (CPAA) progress to develop AT or AU and have an estimated 0% chance of spontaneous recovery [ ]. Longer disease duration confers a reduced response to treatment with JAKi, though the response to treatment is seen even in patients with a disease episode of over 4 years. The duration of the AA episode does not appear to affect the speed of response to treatment [ ]. 3.5 When to Stop or Titrate Down Treatment A study evaluating relapse rates following treatment withdrawal in patients who achieved a SALT score of ≤ 20 with baricitinib ( n = 40) and maintained their response for 1 year found that 20% of patients sustained their response 3 years after discontinuation. Upon retreatment, most patients regained clinical response. Notably, patients who remained in remission for 3 years had a shorter current episode duration and shorter disease duration [ ]. Similarly, for patients who were successfully treated with ritlecitinib for 6 months, defined as a 30% improvement in SALT score ( n = 22), 18% (4/22) of patients maintained response 28 weeks post‐discontinuation [ ]. As approximately one‐fifth of patients remain in remission after treatment withdrawal, discontinuation of JAK inhibitor therapy may be considered after 6–12 months of treatment in patients who have achieved their target response. Alternatively, gradual dose tapering can be considered where feasible. The decision should be made in discussion with the patient, ensuring they are fully informed of the potential consequences of continuing, stopping or reducing the dose. 3.5.1 Interclass Switching Treatment failure with one JAKi does not necessarily predict treatment failure with a another. Emerging evidence has shown that patients that failed to respond to the pan JAKi, tofacitinib, may respond to treatment with baricitinib or ruxolitinib. These findings support the feasibility of interclass switching and suggest that trialling a different JAKi may be a reasonable strategy in non‐responders [ , , ]. 4 Guidelines for Treatment Initiation, Monitoring and Management With JAK Inhibitors Prior to initiating JAK inhibitor (JAKi) therapy, patients should be assessed for risk factors that may increase the likelihood of morbidity or mortality with JAKi therapy (see Table ). Although the only absolute contraindications in current drug prescribing information to JAKis are hypersensitivity to the drug or its excipients and active serious or opportunistic infections, other clinical conditions may warrant caution or even avoidance of treatment (Table ). Although not explicitly listed as absolute contraindications in the current prescribing information, their presence should prompt a careful individualised risk–benefit assessment. Recommended laboratory testing before and during JAKi therapy is outlined in Table . 4.1 Vaccinations Live vaccines are generally contraindicated immediately before and after treatment with JAKi, and if indicated should be received at least 1 month before starting immunosuppressive therapy [ ]. Completion of all age‐appropriate immunisation is recommended prior to treatment initiation, as well as: Recombinant herpes zoster vaccine Influenza vaccine Pneumococcal vaccine COVID‐19 vaccine For vaccines given as a series (Shingrix), the first dose should ideally be given before starting therapy to ensure the best response, unless this would cause a significant delay in the start of a necessary treatment. All non‐live vaccinations recommended prior to treatment can be given safely during therapy if necessary. Administration of adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine in rheumatoid arthritis patients treated with JAKi resulted in significant increases in anti‐varicella‐zoster virus immunoglobulin G titers [ , , , ]. 4.2 Indications for Interruption of Treatment Treatment should be interrupted and restarted when values/status return to normal [ , ]. Absolute lymphocyte count < 500/mm 3 Haemoglobin < 8 g/dL Absolute neutrophil count < 1000 cells/mm 3 Serious infection or opportunistic infection Liver function tests show elevations of ≥ 3 times the upper limit of normal In case of herpes zoster infection developing while on treatment, temporary interruption of treatment may be considered Treatment should be discontinued: Platelet count < 50,000/mm 3 4.3 AA Flare‐Up During Treatment During treatment, some patients may experience disease flare‐up with new onset of discrete alopecic patches. Such cases can be managed by increasing the dose of JAKi if on baricitinib 2 mg daily dose (increase to 4 mg daily). Intralesional steroid injections if limited involvement, or in cases of extensive exacerbation, initiation of a

opportunistic infection Liver function tests show elevations of ≥ 3 times the upper limit of normal In case of herpes zoster infection developing while on treatment, temporary interruption of treatment may be considered Treatment should be discontinued: Platelet count < 50,000/mm 3 4.3 AA Flare‐Up During Treatment During treatment, some patients may experience disease flare‐up with new onset of discrete alopecic patches. Such cases can be managed by increasing the dose of JAKi if on baricitinib 2 mg daily dose (increase to 4 mg daily). Intralesional steroid injections if limited involvement, or in cases of extensive exacerbation, initiation of a short course of concomitant systemic corticosteroids, with gradual tapering. 4.4 Adjuvant Minoxidil Therapy A synergistic effect has been demonstrated when incorporating minoxidil with JAKi treatment [ , ]. A recent systematic review, found increased efficacy when combining oral minoxidil with JAKi (85%) [ ]. 5 Systemic Corticosteroids (Level of Evidence B) Prednisolone or similar systemic corticosteroids are currently considered first‐line treatment for acute moderate to very severe AA. Treatment can be administered orally, intramuscularly or intravenously as pulse therapy [ , , , ]. A trial of systemic steroids can be considered for chronic moderate to very severe AA. Relapse on dose reduction or cessation of treatment is common; however, severe short‐term and cumulative toxicity preclude their use for more than 3 months. Therapeutic protocols and effectiveness vary across studies and there is no evidence to clearly rank the various systemic steroid agents or therapeutic protocols. In the Alopecia Areata Consensus of Experts (ACE) study, prednisolone was the preferred systemic corticosteroid, with once daily mane administration [ ] starting with a dose of 0.4–0.6 mg/kg/day with gradual tapering off over 6–12 weeks. Pre‐screening investigations for untreated infections should be considered to minimise the steroid‐related complications. Patients on treatment should be monitored regularly for sleep and mood disturbance, diabetes, hypertension, peptic ulcer disease, ocular toxicity and acute infections. Prophylaxis against osteopenia should also be considered. 6 Ciclosporin (Level of Evidence C) To date, there is only one RCT that has investigated the efficacy of ciclosporin (CSA) monotherapy in AA [ ]. In this double‐blind, randomised, placebo‐controlled study, 32 patients (18–65 years) with moderate–severe AA were randomised to receive either CSA (4 mg/kg/day) or placebo for 3 months. Although the proportion of patients achieving a 50% reduction in the SALT score was higher in the ciclosporin group (31.3%) compared to the placebo group (6.3%), the results were not statistically significant ( p = 0.07). A 2021 meta‐analysis assessing the therapeutic efficacy of CSA in AA incorporated seven studies evaluating CSA monotherapy and eight studies examining combination with systemic corticosteroids. The authors' assessment was that CSA exhibits a beneficial therapeutic impact on AA. The overall mean proportion of responders, defined as terminal hair growth exceeding 50%, was 73% (95% CI, 57%–85%), with a mean recurrence rate of 39% (95% CI, 10%–78%). The mean response rate for CSA monotherapy was 66% (95% CI, 50%–79%), whereas combination therapy with corticosteroids showed a response rate of 78% (95% CI, 48%–93%). Recurrence rates were 55% (95% CI, 6%–96%) for monotherapy and 28% (95% CI, 6%–72%) for combination therapy [ ]. In the ACE study, it was agreed that CSA is an effective monotherapy agent in AA, with a recommended dose of 3–5 mg/kg/day for a maximum treatment duration of 6–12 months [ ]. CSA, however, is not TGA‐approved for the treatment of AA and based on the current evidence, its use as a first‐line therapy is not recommended by this group. Where other first‐line therapies are not available, or contraindicated, it can be used as a second‐line (off‐label) treatment, either as a monotherapy or in combination with systemic steroids as a steroid‐sparing agent in patients who respond initially to systemic steroids but relapse on dose reduction. 7 Methotrexate (Level of Evidence C) There have been no randomised, placebo‐controlled studies investigating methotrexate (MTX) in AA. In view of the significant rate of spontaneous remission seen in patients with acute and chronic AA, it cannot be assumed that MTX is superior to placebo. Nevertheless, a 2019 meta‐analysis of 16 studies concluded that MTX was an effective treatment for AA [ ]. The overall rate of complete hair regrowth with MTX was 35.8% (95% CI, 25.0%–48.3%). Subgroup analysis revealed that the pooled complete response rate in adults was 44.7% (95% CI, 32.9%–57.1%), significantly higher than the 11.6% (95% CI, 5.1%–24.5%) observed in the paediatric population ( p = 0.001). A recent 2023 double‐blinded RCT of 89 patients with chronic and refractory AT and AU evaluated the efficacy and tolerance of MTX, both as monotherapy (25 mg/week) and in combination with low‐dose prednisone (20 mg/day for 3 months, then 15 mg/day for 3 months) [ ]. At the end of the 12‐month period, the authors concluded that while MTX alone generally

MTX was 35.8% (95% CI, 25.0%–48.3%). Subgroup analysis revealed that the pooled complete response rate in adults was 44.7% (95% CI, 32.9%–57.1%), significantly higher than the 11.6% (95% CI, 5.1%–24.5%) observed in the paediatric population ( p = 0.001). A recent 2023 double‐blinded RCT of 89 patients with chronic and refractory AT and AU evaluated the efficacy and tolerance of MTX, both as monotherapy (25 mg/week) and in combination with low‐dose prednisone (20 mg/day for 3 months, then 15 mg/day for 3 months) [ ]. At the end of the 12‐month period, the authors concluded that while MTX alone generally resulted in partial hair regrowth in patients with chronic AT or AU, whereas combining it with low‐dose prednisone led to complete hair regrowth in up to 31% of patients. In the ACE study, it was agreed that the recommended MTX dose for the treatment of AA is 15–20 mg once weekly [ ]. 8 Azathioprine (Level of Evidence D) An open‐label RCT involving 50 patients with AA (SALT score ≥ 10) compared 300 mg weekly azathioprine (AZA) pulse therapy (WAP) to 5 mg betamethasone on 2 consecutive days every week (mini‐pulse therapy) for 4 months [ ]. The authors concluded both treatments to be effective for AA, with 44.52% of patients who received WAP therapy demonstrating hair regrowth. In a Cochrane analysis, these results were of low certainty [ ]. AZA has also been used with success in the paediatric AA population; however, its benefits must be considered against its potential risks [ ]. 9 Topical Therapy Topical therapy can be used as monotherapy or as an adjunctive treatment. 9.1 Topical and Intralesional Steroid Therapy Topical corticosteroids (TCS) are used in cases of limited area of involvement. They can be used as monotherapy or as an adjunctive treatment [ ]. High‐potency TCS have been shown to be more efficacious than low‐potency formulations [ ]. Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (ILK) is a well‐established treatment for limited‐type AA, with response rates ranging from 60% to 95% across 12 studies [ ]. A systematic review and meta‐analysis identified that the optimal regimen for the administration of ILK is at 3–4 weekly intervals for up to 6 months, at concentrations of 2.5–10 mg/mL for the scalp and 2.5–5 mg/mL for the face [ ]. Potential side effects of TCS and ILK include folliculitis, atrophy, striae, telangiectasia and acneiform eruptions [ ]. 9.2 Contact Immunotherapy Topical contact immunotherapy with diphenylcyclopropenone or squaric acid dibutyl ester can promote hair regrowth in patients with AA. A meta‐analysis of 45 studies ( n = 22,227) found that 65% of patients showed some improvement, with 32.3% achieving complete regrowth with a 49% recurrence rate. However, most studies were not randomised, placebo‐controlled trials, which limit the strength of the evidence [ ]. As the mechanism of action relies on inducing allergic contact dermatitis, side effects are common. These include local erythema, eczematous reactions (e.g., blistering, scaling, exudation), pruritus, regional lymphadenopathy, generalised eczema, hyperpigmentation and flu‐like symptoms [ , ]. 9.3 Topical Calcineurin Inhibitors Topical calcineurin inhibitors are not considered a first‐line treatment for AA at present, as there is no evidence of clinical benefit [ , , ]. 9.4 Topical JAK Inhibitors Topical JAK inhibitors are a potential new treatment for AA with limited effectiveness [ ]. A study conducted by Bokhari et al. involved applying 2% tofacitinib, 1% ruxolitinib, 0.005% topical clobetasol dipropionate and a placebo to the four scalp quadrants of 16 patients with AU for 28 weeks. Partial hair regrowth was observed in the tofacitinib (6/16), ruxolitinib (5/16) and clobetasol (10/16) groups, but not in the placebo group (0/16) [ ]. In an open‐label, single‐arm pilot study, Liu et al. assessed the efficacy and safety of topical tofacitinib in 10 patients with AA. Regrowth occurred in 3 patients (significant regrowth in 1 patient with 61% regrowth and partial regrowth of 35% in 2 patients), whereas seven patients experienced no regrowth [ ]. Topical ruxolitinib and delgocitinib were investigated with unsatisfactory results [ , ]. We currently do not advocate using topical JAKi for scalp AA. 9.5 Topical Minoxidil Topical minoxidil can induce accelerated hair regrowth in alopecia patches and reduce disease activity in AA cases by lowering perifollicular lymphocytic infiltration [ ]. The most common side effect is skin irritation [ , ]. Topical minoxidil has inconclusive evidence to support its use as an adjunct therapy in AA [ ]. 9.6 Topical Prostaglandin Analogues Several studies have explored the efficacy of bimatoprost and latanoprost for scalp alopecia areata, with mixed results [ , ]. Improved efficacy was seen when combined with topical betamethasone or clobetasol [ , ]. 10 Emerging Treatments for AA Several JAK inhibitors are in phase 1, 2 and 3 clinical trials for chronic severe and very severe AA. Notable agents under investigation include tofacitinib,

lymphocytic infiltration [ ]. The most common side effect is skin irritation [ , ]. Topical minoxidil has inconclusive evidence to support its use as an adjunct therapy in AA [ ]. 9.6 Topical Prostaglandin Analogues Several studies have explored the efficacy of bimatoprost and latanoprost for scalp alopecia areata, with mixed results [ , ]. Improved efficacy was seen when combined with topical betamethasone or clobetasol [ , ]. 10 Emerging Treatments for AA Several JAK inhibitors are in phase 1, 2 and 3 clinical trials for chronic severe and very severe AA. Notable agents under investigation include tofacitinib, brepocitinib, deuruxolitinib, ruxolitinib, deucravacitinib, upadacitinib, jaktinib and ivarmacitinib. Tofacitinib, a pan‐JAK inhibitor, is used in both oral and sublingual preparations for AA. A meta‐analysis showed a 54% significant hair regrowth rate, but a high relapse rate after cessation [ ]. Oral tofacitinib is given at a twice‐daily dose. Sublingual tofacitinib offers pharmacokinetic benefits and a longer half‐life, potentially allowing once‐daily dosing [ ]. Brepocitinib, a selective TYK2 and JAK1 inhibitor, was evaluated against ritlecitinib in a phase 2a RCT with 142 participants [ ]. At 24 weeks, 60% of brepocitinib users and 50% of ritlecitinib users achieved a 30% improvement in SALT scores, versus 2% in the placebo group. In addition, 81% reported eyelash regrowth and 72% observed improvements in eyebrows. Ruxolitinib, a selective reversible JAK1/2 inhibitor, has shown effectiveness in treating moderate‐to‐severe AA across various case series [ , ]. In an open‐label study of 75 patients, both ruxolitinib and tofacitinib achieved similar rates of complete remission (21%). However, 84.2% of patients on ruxolitinib reached SALT50 or better, versus 78.4% on tofacitinib [ ]. Deuruxolitinib, a deuterated form of ruxolitinib, approved by the FDA since July 2024 for treatment of severe AA, demonstrated significant improvements in SALT scores in phase 3 studies. At 24 weeks, 42% of patients in the 12 mg group achieved a SALT score of < 20 [ ]. Upadacitinib, a JAK1 inhibitor, is being evaluated in a phase 3 trial in adults and adolescents [ ]. Data from case reports and retrospective cohort studies suggest upadacitinib is effective in treating AA, particularly in patients with concurrent atopic dermatitis [ , , ]. One study involving 25 patients demonstrated a median SALT score improving from 50 to 5 after 24 weeks of treatment [ ]. Another study with 19 patients showed that 57.1% achieved complete hair regrowth at 28 weeks [ ]. Jaktinib, a novel JAK1/2 inhibitor previously evaluated for myelofibrosis, is in a phase 3 RCT for severe AA [ ]. Ivarmacitinib, a JAK1 inhibitor, has shown promising outcomes in a phase 2 RCT involving adults with moderate‐to‐severe AA [ ]. After 24 weeks, the percentage reduction in SALT score from baseline was 19% in the placebo group compared to 56% in patients receiving 4 mg ivarmacitinib daily. Filgotinib is a JAKi with high selectivity for JAK‐1. It is approved by the FDA and EMA (European Medicines Agency) for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and has also been investigated for use in Crohn's disease. Complete scalp hair regrowth was reported in a patient with severe alopecia areata who received filgotinib as part of a clinical trial evaluating its efficacy in Crohn's disease [ ]. Deucravacitinib, a TYK2 inhibitor, approved by the TGA for the treatment of psoriasis, is undergoing phase 2 clinical trials to assess its effectiveness in treating AA [ ]. 10.1 Biologics Dupilumab, an IL‐4Rα blocker approved for atopic dermatitis, may exert therapeutic effects in alopecia areata through modulating the Th2‐pathway signalling [ ]. In a phase 2a RCT involving 60 patients (23 patients with AD), 32.5% achieved SALT30, 22.5% SALT50 and 15% SALT75 by week 48. A significant correlation was observed between elevated baseline IgE levels and response to treatment [ ]. In contrast, there are also case reports suggesting that dupilumab may paradoxically induce or exacerbate AA in certain individuals [ , , ]. Tralokinumab, an IL‐13 inhibitor, has shown effectiveness in a case study in mild to moderate AA patients with AD treatment [ ]. Several immunomodulating agents are in phase 2 trials for AA, including daxdilimab (ILT7 target), rosnilimab (PD‐1 agonist), etrasimod (SJP receptor modulator), EQ101 (tri‐specific IL‐2, IL‐9, IL‐15 antagonist) and bempikibart (IL‐7/TSLP receptor antagonist) [ , , , , ]. Apremilast, a PDE‐4 inhibitor that reduces IFN‐γ activity, has been described in the treatment of AA; however, case series in which its use in AA has been described have revealed inconsistent effectiveness [ , , , , ]. 10.2 Off Label Indications for Systemic Treatment—Facial Alopecia Areata Baricitinib, ritlecitinib and brepocitinib have shown efficacy in promoting eyebrow and eyelash regrowth through phase 2–3 RCTs [ , , ]. Tofacitinib has also shown effectiveness in a large case series [ ]. Interestingly, the duration of eyebrow and eyelash

IL‐15 antagonist) and bempikibart (IL‐7/TSLP receptor antagonist) [ , , , , ]. Apremilast, a PDE‐4 inhibitor that reduces IFN‐γ activity, has been described in the treatment of AA; however, case series in which its use in AA has been described have revealed inconsistent effectiveness [ , , , , ]. 10.2 Off Label Indications for Systemic Treatment—Facial Alopecia Areata Baricitinib, ritlecitinib and brepocitinib have shown efficacy in promoting eyebrow and eyelash regrowth through phase 2–3 RCTs [ , , ]. Tofacitinib has also shown effectiveness in a large case series [ ]. Interestingly, the duration of eyebrow and eyelash loss did not significantly impact treatment outcomes, indicating these hair follicles may remain viable even after extended periods of inactivity. Topical tofacitinib and ruxolitinib have shown promise in smaller studies [ , , , ]. An eDelphi study found that systemic therapy is warranted for AA affecting eyebrows or eyelashes if it leads to functional or occupational impairment [ ]. Beard alopecia areata (BAA) can have profound psychosocial effects [ ]. Baricitinib, tofacitinib and ruxolitinib have been used successfully in case reports and small case series, though their efficacy in BAA has not been studied in RCTs [ , , ]. Prostaglandin analogues including bimatoprost and latanoprost have been shown to induce eyelash regrowth in several studies [ , , , , , , ]. 10.3 Patient Registries Given the need to understand the safety profile of emerging therapies and better describe the real‐world effectiveness of existing and emerging mono and combination treatment regimens, the group strongly advocates for the registration of patients in high‐quality patient registries. This concept has been supported internationally and has led to the development of the Global Registry of Alopecia Areata Disease Severity and Treatment Safety (GRASS) [ , ]. The pilot phase of this project has been led by the Australasian Hair and Wool Research Society and National and International Registry Solutions (NISR), an Irish charity, in Australia over the past 3 years, but has also established sites in Ireland and Italy, with multiple other international centres in the process of joining to provide comparable, harmonised data that will facilitate the development of valuable networks to help gather and interpret data from the use of therapies in AA. 11 Conclusion Guidelines for the management of moderate to very severe alopecia areata in paediatric and adolescent populations are needed; however, this was beyond the scope of the current work. Given the accumulating evidence demonstrating the limited efficacy, higher cost and unfavourable side effect profiles of immunosuppressants such as MTX, CSA and AZA, we recommend reserving these treatments for cases in which systemic treatment is warranted but JAKi are contraindicated. Emerging data suggest that early initiation of treatment is associated with improved response rates and prognosis. Therefore, JAKi should be considered for patients with a SALT score of 21 and higher corresponding with moderate‐to‐severe severity. In cases of eyelash or eyebrow involvement, initiation of JAKi therapy may also be appropriate at lower SALT scores. chunks.content: 1 Introduction In recent years, cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs), including pacemakers (PMs) and implantable cardioverter‐defibrillators (ICDs), have become an essential component of arrhythmia management in pediatric patients. Alongside technological advances in device therapy, remote monitoring (RM) has developed into an important tool that enables continuous device surveillance and early identification of clinically significant events, including arrhythmias and device‐related abnormalities, prior to scheduled in‐person evaluations (IPEs). Current international consensus documents and recommendations—including the 2021 PACES Expert Consensus Statement on CIEDs in Pediatric Patients [ ] and the 2023 HRS/EHRA/APHRS/LAHRS Expert Consensus on Practical Management of the Remote Device Clinic [ ] – recommend RM as the standard component of CIED follow‐up in all eligible patients. The application of RM in the pediatric population presents specific challenges that distinguish it from adult practice. Symptom recognition is frequently limited due to young age, atypical clinical presentation, or neurodevelopmental conditions, increasing the likelihood of clinically silent arrhythmias remaining undetected between scheduled visits. As per the available literature, even up to 39% of arrhythmic events in children with CIEDs may be asymptomatic, and the RM alert can precede a scheduled IPE by more than 100 days [ ] Moreover, the RM system is also associated with high levels of parental satisfaction [ , ]. Despite these encouraging data, and notwithstanding robust evidence from large adult cohorts demonstrating clinical advantages of RM in adult populations [ , ], the evidence base for RM in pediatric CIED patients remains limited and largely derived from small, single‐center observational studies. Standardized protocols for alert programming, transmission frequency, and clinical response remain inconsistent across centers. In this context, focused clinical observations from institutions with established RM programs may provide additional real‐world insight into how RM influences clinical decision‐making—particularly in patients who are asymptomatic or unable to self‐report—and may inform future prospective studies in this population. 2 Methods Data from patients with PM or ICD and RM were retrospectively reviewed. Three representative cases were selected to illustrate the clinical utility of RM in detecting arrhythmias and guiding timely interventions. Clinical histories, device settings, and RM transmissions were analyzed through electronic medical records and a dedicated remote monitoring service. CIED follow‐up included IPE every three months. RM alerts were transmitted automatically to the assigned clinician based on predefined device‐specific parameters (Table ). Alerts were classified by severity (either yellow or red), and clinical response was initiated promptly upon review of critical transmissions. RM alert criteria and their color‐coded severity levels were predefined by the clinician during patient enrollment. Yellow alerts triggered an automated e‐mail notification, whereas red alerts were delivered as direct text messages to the clinician's mobile device. To optimize clinical workflow, patient RM devices most often synchronized with the RM system during the night, resulting in alert delivery to the clinician in the morning. Device programming, RM threshold, and alert management were consistent with institutional protocols and manufacturer recommendations. All interventions and clinical decisions were guided by the RM data in conjunction with standard pediatric cardiology care. 2.1 Case Presentation 2.1.1 Case 1 A 16‐year‐old male with an intellectual disability was referred for evaluation of a prolonged QTc interval on the electrocardiogram (ECG). He had a history of two spontaneous syncopal episodes. Subsequent workup revealed long‐QT syndrome (LQTS), paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF), and left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) on echocardiography. Given the combination of LQTS, LVH, and recurrent syncope of unknown etiology, ICD implantation was indicated. A dual‐chamber transvenous ICD was implanted and enrolled in the institutional RM system. During follow‐up, RM transmitted multiple recordings of self‐terminating AF. One transmission captured a critical event: AF degenerating into ventricular fibrillation (VF), terminated by two consecutive ICD shocks (Figure ). The patient reported neither the arrhythmia nor the shock delivery. His parents remained unaware of the event until notified by the supervising physician following RM alert review. Due to the patient's intellectual disability, symptom‐based detection was not a reliable monitoring strategy. RM represented the only viable means of real‐time arrhythmia surveillance in this patient. 2.1.1.1 Clinical Takeaway In patients with neurodevelopmental conditions or intellectual disability, RM may represent the only reliable mechanism for detecting life‐threatening arrhythmias and initiating a timely clinical response. 2.1.2 Case 2 A 6‐year‐old male with surgically corrected tetralogy of Fallot (ToF) and pulmonary valve atresia was hospitalized following an incidentally observed nocturnal bradycardia. Holter monitoring confirmed sick sinus syndrome (SSS) and persistent atrial flutter (AFL). Notably, the patient remained entirely asymptomatic throughout. Sequential antiarrhythmic therapy—initially amiodarone, subsequently propranolol—failed to maintain sinus rhythm and further exacerbated the underlying bradycardia, making continued pharmacological management untenable. PM implantation was therefore indicated. Given the patient's young age, small body size, and prior sternotomy with associated pericardial adhesions, a transvenous approach was precluded. of Fallot (ToF) and pulmonary valve atresia was hospitalized following an incidentally observed nocturnal bradycardia. Holter monitoring confirmed sick sinus syndrome (SSS) and persistent atrial flutter (AFL). Notably, the patient remained entirely asymptomatic throughout. Sequential antiarrhythmic therapy—initially amiodarone, subsequently propranolol—failed to maintain sinus rhythm and further exacerbated the underlying bradycardia, making continued pharmacological management untenable. PM implantation was therefore indicated. Given the patient's young age, small body size, and prior sternotomy with associated pericardial adhesions, a transvenous approach was precluded. Epicardial lead implantation was performed via redo sternotomy using suture‐on epicardial leads. Suture‐on leads are the only type used at our center for epicardial pacing in pediatric patients, as from our center's experience, screw‐in epicardial leads are associated with higher complication rates and are therefore avoided. A dual‐chamber epicardial PM was implanted and enrolled in the RM program. RM transmissions during follow‐up included multiple episodes of atrial tachycardia (AT), the majority of which were self‐terminating and clinically evaluated as consistent with AFL. One transmission captured an atrial rate of 250 bpm with automatic mode switch to permanent ventricular pacing, indicating hemodynamically significant AFL without spontaneous termination (Figure ). No symptoms were reported. Following alert review, the supervising physician contacted the family, confirmed the diagnosis based on RM data, and arranged prompt electrical cardioversion. Because AFL was confirmed via RM prior to admission, empirical anticoagulation and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) were deemed unnecessary, reducing diagnostic workload and shortening the length of hospitalization. 2.1.2.1 Clinical Takeaway RM‐guided pre‐admission arrhythmia confirmation may streamline acute management by allowing clinical preparation before the patient arrives and may reduce the need for invasive or time‐consuming diagnostic procedures. 2.1.3 Case 3 A 2‐year‐old male presented with recurrent episodes of AFL, characterized by a predominantly 2:1 block with an atrial rhythm of 280 bpm, and intermittent 4:1 or 5:1 conduction ratios. The patient was asymptomatic. Combined antiarrhythmic therapy, including electrical cardioversion and amiodarone, failed to achieve a sustained sinus rhythm. Diagnostic workup confirmed SSS, with a 24‐h Holter monitoring revealing sinus pauses of up to 5 s. PM implantation was indicated. As in Case 2, the patient's age and anatomical constraints precluded a transvenous approach. Epicardial PM implantation was performed using suture‐on epicardial leads, consistent with the institutional protocol described above. The device was enrolled in daily RM. RM transmissions during follow‐up included multiple self‐terminating episodes of AT. Three RM‐triggered alerts, however, were evaluated as consistent with AFL and prompted emergency hospitalization, each followed by electrical cardioversion and initiation of metoprolol therapy (Figure ). In each instance, RM alert data provided advance confirmation of the arrhythmia prior to the patient's arrival, enabling the clinical team to prepare for cardioversion without additional diagnostic delay. Anticoagulation and TEE were not required, similar to the approach described in Case 2. 2.1.3.1 Clinical Takeaway Even in the youngest pediatric patients, in whom symptom‐based reporting is inherently impossible, daily RM enables prompt arrhythmia recognition and facilitates a structured, prepared clinical response at the time of admission. 3 Discussion The three cases presented here illustrate specific clinical scenarios in which daily, alert‐based RM of CIEDs enabled timely recognition and response to significant arrhythmic events in pediatric patients who were either asymptomatic or unable to self‐report their symptoms. While three cases cannot demonstrate the effectiveness of RM as a clinical tool, they highlight a clinically important pattern—one that is consistent with, and contextualized by, the growing body of evidence supporting RM in the pediatric CIED population. 3.1 Asymptomatic Arrhythmias and the Limitations of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">IPE</styled-content> A recurring and clinically critical theme across all three cases is the complete absence of symptom perception or inability to properly manifest them. In Case 1, an episode of AF degenerating into VF—terminated by ICD shock—went unrecognized by both the patient and his family. In Cases 2 and 3, hemodynamically significant AFL with mode‐switch triggered no reportable symptoms in either a 6‐year‐old or a 2‐year‐old. This pattern is well‐documented in the literature. Malloy et al. [ ] found that 39% of adverse events were asymptomatic, and that RM detected clinically significant events a median of 134 days earlier than would have been possible under a biannual IPE schedule. Maldonado et al. [ ] in a long‐term follow‐up of 27 children with CIEDs reported five patients with red‐level alerts, three of which corresponded to arrhythmias in the VF monitoring zone, with two patients receiving appropriate shocks—a scenario directly paralleled by Case 1 in the present report. Taken together, these findings reinforce the premise that in young patients, and particularly in those with neurodevelopmental conditions, reliance on symptom‐based detection is insufficient as the sole monitoring strategy, and that continuous device surveillance is a necessary—rather than supplementary—component of the follow‐up. 3.2 Clinical Impact of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">RM</styled-content>‐Guided Intervention Beyond arrhythmia detection, RM in Cases 2 and 3 had a direct and measurable impact

with CIEDs reported five patients with red‐level alerts, three of which corresponded to arrhythmias in the VF monitoring zone, with two patients receiving appropriate shocks—a scenario directly paralleled by Case 1 in the present report. Taken together, these findings reinforce the premise that in young patients, and particularly in those with neurodevelopmental conditions, reliance on symptom‐based detection is insufficient as the sole monitoring strategy, and that continuous device surveillance is a necessary—rather than supplementary—component of the follow‐up. 3.2 Clinical Impact of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">RM</styled-content>‐Guided Intervention Beyond arrhythmia detection, RM in Cases 2 and 3 had a direct and measurable impact on the clinical management pathway. In both cases, advance confirmation of AFL via RM prior to hospital admission allowed the clinical team to prepare for electrical cardioversion without the need for empirical anticoagulation or TEE. This is consistent with observations by Jouen et al. [ ]., who reported that in a cohort of 34 pediatric patients under RM, all cases requiring hospitalization were managed within 24 h of alert transmission, attributing this to the advanced clinical information provided by the RM system. The ability to confirm arrhythmia diagnosis remotely before admission has practical implications beyond time‐to‐treatment: It reduces procedural burden, shortens hospitalization, and—in young children—minimizes exposure to sedation and invasive diagnostics that would otherwise be required for pre‐cardioversion workup. 3.3 Alert Programming An important practical consideration in any RM program is the signal‐to‐noise ratio of alert transmissions, as inappropriate alert burden risks clinician data overload and delayed response to true arrhythmic events. In the pediatric context, the most common source of false‐positive yellow alerts in our experience is sinus tachycardia triggered by crying, agitation, or febrile illness, which may transiently exceed rate‐based thresholds programmed for pathological tachyarrhythmia detection. At our center, alert thresholds are individually configured for each patient according to their clinical profile, device type, and underlying diagnosis—an approach consistent with current consensus recommendations for individualized RM programming [ ]. Alert evaluation and clinical response decisions remain the responsibility of a single designated physician. 3.4 Parental Engagement and Remote Follow‐Up Acceptability An underappreciated dimension of RM in pediatric practice is its impact on families. In all three cases, parents were the primary point of contact following RM alert review, and in Cases 1 and 2, they were notified of significant arrhythmic events of which they had been entirely unaware. Leoni et al. [ ] reported that all enrolled patients and their parents expressed high satisfaction with RM as an alternative to more frequent IPE. Spentzou et al. [ ]. Similarly reported high parental satisfaction with virtual pacing clinics for children with CIEDs. These observations are clinically relevant: Parental engagement and confidence in the monitoring system are prerequisites for the consistent connectivity on which RM depends. In our experience, clear communication with families regarding the alert system—including the distinction between red and yellow alerts and the expected clinical response—is an essential component of RM program implementation. 3.5 Limitations and Future Directions Several limitations of this report must be acknowledged. The three cases were selected to specifically illustrate the clinical impact of RM‐triggered alerts in patients unable to self‐report symptoms and are therefore not representative of the full spectrum of RM transmissions from our center's cohort. Standardized outcome data—including time from alert to clinical intervention, alert volume, and hospitalization rates—would be required to quantify the benefit of RM and are not available from the present report, given its descriptive scope. Our center maintains an ongoing prospective registry of all pediatric patients with CIEDs under RM, and a comprehensive cohort analysis—including demographics, device characteristics, alert frequency, actionability rates, and clinical outcomes—is planned as a subsequent study, for which the present cases provide clinical context and preliminary observations. 4 Conclusions RM represents a valuable component of follow‐up care for pediatric patients with CIEDs, particularly in those who are asymptomatic or unable to report their symptoms. The cases presented illustrate how RM may enable timely arrhythmia recognition, guide clinical decision‐making prior to hospital admission, and reduce the diagnostic burden associated with arrhythmic events. As the evidence base for pediatric CIED RM continues to grow, prospective cohort studies with standardized outcome reporting will be essential to define its full clinical benefit in this population. Van Wagoner, PhD, FAHA, FHRS AIM: The “2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation” provides recommendations to guide clinicians in the treatment of patients with atrial fibrillation. METHODS: A comprehensive literature search was conducted from May 12, 2022, to November 3, 2022, encompassing studies, reviews, and other evidence conducted on human subjects that were published in English from PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, and other selected databases relevant to this guideline. Additional relevant studies, published through November 2022, during the guideline writing process, were also considered by the writing committee and added to the evidence tables, where appropriate. *Writing committee members are required to recuse themselves from voting on sections to which their specific relationships with industry may apply; see Appendix 1 for detailed information. †ACC/AHA Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines liaison. ‡ACC/AHA Joint Committee on Performance Measures liaison. §Lay stakeholder representative. ‖American College of Clinical Pharmacy representative. ¶Heart Rhythm Society representative. #Joint ACC/AHA staff representative. **ACC/AHA Joint Committee on Clinical Data Standards liaison. DOI: 10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193  January 2, 2024 e1 Joglar et al 2023 Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation STRUCTURE: Atrial fibrillation is the most sustained common arrhythmia, and its incidence and prevalence are increasing in the CLINICAL STATEMENTS United States and globally. Recommendations from the “2014 AHA/ACC/HRS Guideline for the Management of Patients AND GUIDELINES With Atrial Fibrillation” and the “2019 AHA/ACC/HRS Focused Update of the 2014 AHA/ACC/HRS Guideline for the Management of Patients With Atrial Fibrillation” have been updated with new evidence to guide clinicians. In addition, new recommendations addressing atrial fibrillation and thromboembolic risk assessment, anticoagulation, left atrial appendage occlusion, atrial fibrillation catheter or surgical ablation, and risk factor modification and atrial fibrillation prevention have been developed. AF can be documented by, for example, 12-lead ECG, rhythm strips, wearables, intracardiac electrograms, but will always require visual confirmation that the diagnosis is accurate. Clinical AF With the increasing availability of wearable devices and other continuous monitoring technologies, the distinction between clinical and subclinical AF has become increasingly blurred, thus the writing committee felt the term clinical AF has become less useful. Yet, the term was kept because most of the evidence from randomized trials that have led to guideline recommendations for the treatment of AF refer to “clinical AF.” These trials required electrocardiographic documentation of the arrhythmia for inclusion and most patients presented for clinical evaluation and/or therapy of the arrhythmia. Subclinical AF Subclinical AF refers to this arrhythmia identified in individuals who do not have symptoms attributable to AF and in whom there are no previous ECGs documenting AF This includes AF identified by implanted devices (pacemakers, defibrillators, or implantable loop recorders) or wearable monitors Atrial high-rate These are defined as atrial events exceeding the programmed detection rate limit set by the device. These are recorded by implanted episodes devices but require visual inspection to confirm AF and exclude other atrial arrhythmias, artifact or oversensing. AF burden AF burden encompasses both frequency and duration and refers to the amount of AF that an individual has. AF burden has been defined differently across studies. For the purpose of this guideline, AF burden will be defined as the durations of an an episode or as a percentage of AF duration during the monitoring period depending on how it was defined in the individual studies.
